diagnosis.summary: The order-service Lambda handler is running far slower than normal, with mean execution time up 176x and end-to-end latency up sharply across all percentiles. The degradation has persisted for 3 minutes with no error traffic and a flat request rate, indicating a pure performance regression inside the function. No 5xx errors have been observed so far.
diagnosis.root_cause: Severe slowdown of the order-service Lambda handler body is the most likely root cause, with mean CPU time rising from 2 ms to 352 ms and end-to-end latency following proportionally, while traffic and error rates remain unchanged.
evidence: Mean Lambda handler duration rose from 2 ms to 352 ms, a 176x increase.
Median end-to-end latency rose from 17 ms to 360 ms, a 21x increase.
p95 end-to-end latency rose from 24 ms to 375 ms, a 15.6x increase above baseline.
Request rate is flat at 2.9 rps against a baseline of 2.9 rps, ruling out a traffic surge as an explanation.
5xx error rate remains at 0.0, so requests are completing but slowly.
recommended_actions: Inspect order-service Lambda CloudWatch Logs for the current window to identify any slow operations, unexpected loops, or blocking calls inside the handler.
Check order-service dependency metrics toward payment-service to determine whether slow outbound calls to payment-service are inflating handler time.
Review order-service DynamoDB latency metrics to determine whether database calls within the handler are slower than normal.
Check cold_start_count for order-service to determine whether cold starts are contributing to the elevated handler duration.
If a recent function deployment or configuration change coincides with the start of the incident, consider rolling it back.

findings: evidence[3]: causal wording 'ruling out'; correlated timestamps are an observed sequence, not proof of cause
